endorsements.quote: For high-risk systems, evaluation should progress from retrospective validation to external validation, prospective silent trial, workflow evaluation, and monitored deployment.
Documentation should include model cards, dataset documentation, risk-management artifacts, and change-control processes [5], [6], [17]–[19].

Health systems should require vendors to produce FHIRTrustBench-scored profiles before procurement, with particular attention to AI Validation and Governance Readiness, the two dimensions the benchmark pool scored most consistently weak.
A system should advance to routine clinical use not because it connects to a FHIR endpoint, but only when all five dimensions are jointly sufficient for the intended risk class.

unlisted_practices: Developers should engineer and test FHIR integration as part of the model pipeline, not as a deployment wrapper.

Report AI metrics and interoperability metrics together, including FHIR version, implementation guide, resource profiles, value sets, terminology mappings, provenance completeness, SMART scopes, CDS trigger, and missingness.
Regulators should incorporate interoperability dimension evidence into algorithm transparency and post-market monitoring requirements.
Treat interoperability assurance as a pre-model safety gate evaluating FHIR implementation quality, terminology, units, and provenance before AI validation.
Test AI robustness to missing or shifted FHIR data elements during validation.

screen.reason: Presents a benchmark rubric, deployment lifecycle framework, and reporting checklist for evaluating FHIR-driven clinical AI readiness and trustworthiness, applied here to score a corpus of literature/sources rather than testing an AI system on clinical task data.
